title: Conservative surgical treatment for adenomyosis: New options for looking beyond uterus removal
journal: Best Practice & Research Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology
clinical_background: Adenomyosis is a benign uterine condition in which endometrial glands and stroma occur within the myometrium. It may be focal or cause diffuse uterine enlargement. Affected patients can experience dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) or infertility, although about one third have no symptoms. Sonographic signs occur in about 21% of the general population and are more frequent among women undergoing assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs). Adenomyosis often coexists with endometriosis, uterine myomas or congenital uterine abnormalities; reported coexistence with endometriosis on imaging ranges between 21.2% and 89.4%. Treatment may be medical, radiological or surgical according to symptoms, age and fertility wishes. Hysterectomy remains the only definitive treatment, while interest in preserving the uterus has increased.
interpretation: The authors consider medical, radiological and uterus-preserving surgical treatments capable of improving abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain while reducing uterine size. Hormonal treatment is their primary approach during reproductive life; they consider radiological procedures and conservative surgery when medical treatment fails. Hysterectomy remains the only definitive treatment. Although conservative surgery can be effective, its technical demands and potential obstetric complications are important considerations.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The article contrasts the established definitive role of hysterectomy with published experience of uterus-preserving procedures. Previously reported outcomes suggest that conservative operations improve pelvic pain (>70% at 12 months) and abnormal uterine bleeding (>70% at 12 months), with no significant difference apparent among procedures. Osada et al. reported uterine rupture during pregnancy in 5% of patients previously treated by adenomyomectomy. Published comparisons describe short-term pain improvement after RFA as similar to that after conventional uterus-preserving surgery, while medical treatment appears more effective than hysteroscopy for adenomyosis-related symptoms. Evidence on UAE for adenomyosis comes from case series, unlike the randomized trials cited for uterine leiomyoma.
clinical_implications: Choice of treatment depends on symptoms, age and fertility wishes; preserving the uterus may be particularly important when medical treatment has repeatedly failed.

Adenomyomectomy addresses focal disease, whereas cytoreductive surgery may be used for focal or diffuse disease. Surgery for diffuse disease must balance removal of affected tissue against adequate uterine-wall reconstruction.
Conservative surgery carries possible pregnancy-related risks, including uterine rupture, miscarriage, other pregnancy complications and abnormal placentation.
Concurrent pelvic endometriosis, particularly DE, or uterine myomas may make treatment more complex and require multidisciplinary care.
The reported benefits and complication rates of complex surgery may not apply equally outside highly experienced centres.
practice_implications: Use medical treatment as the initial approach and consider UAE, HIFU, RFA, hysteroscopy or conservative surgery when it fails. The practice points include LNG-IUS, dienogest, GnRH-a and oral GnRH-ants among initial hormonal options, although the treatment discussion describes GnRH-a as second-line when progestins are ineffective or not tolerated.

Individualize uterus-preserving surgery according to patient needs and preoperative assessment of disease location and extent by pelvic ultrasound and MRI; no conservative surgical option has been demonstrated superior.

Have experienced surgeons perform complex conservative operations in dedicated centres, particularly for laparoscopy or concomitant endometriosis. Open surgery may be preferable when palpation is needed to distinguish affected from healthy myometrium.

During conservative surgery, avoid thermal damage to incision margins because it increases the risk of suture dehiscence. Temporary uterine-artery occlusion or ligation, or intramyometrial vasopressin or oxytocin, may be options in some cases to reduce operative blood loss.

Consider RFA or hysteroscopy in selected premenopausal patients with symptomatic focal disease resistant to hormonal treatment. Hysteroscopy is not considered appropriate for deeper lesions; endometrial or endo-myometrial ablation may be performed in women who do not desire future pregnancy.
Hysterectomy remains the definitive surgical option for premenopausal patients who do not wish to preserve the uterus.
limitations: The authors state that complication rates after conservative surgery may be underestimated because the reported techniques come from centres with substantial surgical expertise; some authors question whether those outcomes apply to general gynaecological practice.
Evidence on the effects of RFA on abnormal uterine bleeding, uterine morphology, pregnancy and fertility is inconclusive.
No conservative surgical technique has been demonstrated superior to the others.
The role of hysteroscopy in diagnosis is difficult to establish because it does not examine the deeper myometrium commonly involved in adenomyosis.
open_questions: Which conservative surgical strategy offers the best balance of symptom control, complications and obstetric outcomes?
How durable are improvements in abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain after conservative surgery?
How do conservative surgical outcomes compare with medical treatments, particularly newer GnRH antagonists, and with radiological procedures, particularly RFA?
future_directions: Compare conservative surgical strategies with respect to outcomes, complications and obstetric outcomes.
Evaluate long-term effects of conservative surgery, particularly on abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain.
Compare conservative surgery with medical treatment, especially newer GnRH antagonists.
Compare conservative surgery with radiological procedures, particularly RFA.

GnRH-a: an initial flare-up effect was reported. No rate was provided.
HIFU: skin burns and nerve injury were identified as severe adverse effects or complications. No rates were provided.
Adenomyomectomy: Osada et al. reported uterine rupture during pregnancy in 5% of patients who had previously undergone the procedure.

Conservative surgery: abortion, pregnancy complications and placentation abnormalities, including placenta previa and placenta accreta spectrum, were described without a high prevalence or numerical rates.

RFA: severe complications were described as uncommon and included perforation, infections and thermal injuries of abdominal organs. No rates were provided.

subgroup_analyses: Across the studies cited, HIFU was more effective for focal than diffuse adenomyosis; the review also states that recurrence depends on adenomyosis type.
LNG-IUS treatment failure was significantly higher in women whose uterine volume was greater than 150 mL.
The review reports no significant difference in symptom outcomes among the conservative surgical procedures, without an estimate or p value.
The review describes hysteroscopic treatment as an option for lesions near the endometrium, but not for deeper adenomyotic lesions.
secondary_results: HIFU combined with LNG-IUS was reported to improve clinical outcomes; the cited study in Table 2 reported reductions in uterine volume and blood-flow signal with HIFU combined with LNG-IUD.
The review states that LNG-IUS produces quality-of-life improvements comparable to those of more invasive surgical techniques.
The review describes decreased Qol and impaired sexual life among women with both adenomyosis and endometriosis.

The review reports that RFA-related improvement in pain and AUB is similar to that of conventional uterus-sparing surgery, while evidence concerning its effects on pregnancy and fertility remains inconclusive.

main_conclusion: The authors regard hormonal treatment as the initial approach to adenomyosis and reserve radiological or conservative surgical options for cases in which medical treatment fails. Because uterus-preserving surgery is technically demanding, particularly with concomitant endometriosis, they conclude that experienced surgeons in dedicated centers should perform it.
narrative_summary:
This narrative review examines medical, radiological and uterus-preserving surgical approaches to adenomyosis, emphasizing symptom control, uterine volume and treatment choice. The authors place hormonal therapy first during reproductive life; radiological procedures and conservative surgery are considered when medication fails. UAE is associated with a reported 50% reduction in uterine volume at 12 months after treatment. For HIFU, cited follow-up data report complete symptom relief in 68% of treated women at 2 years, although treatment response varies with the form of adenomyosis.

Among surgical options, adenomyomectomy addresses focal disease, while cytoreductive techniques can address focal or diffuse disease. The review reports improvement in pelvic pain and AUB of >70% at 12 months after conservative surgery and an estimated 3.1-fold reduction in uterine volume; it does not establish that one conservative procedure is superior. Osada et al. reported uterine rupture during pregnancy in 5% of patients after adenomyomectomy. RFA has produced uterine volume reductions ranging from 41% to 57% across cited studies, but evidence concerning fertility and pregnancy remains inconclusive. Hysteroscopic treatment is discussed for lesions close to the endometrium. The authors stress individualized planning, careful uterine reconstruction and specialist surgical experience, especially when endometriosis requires concurrent treatment.

document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Adenomyosis is a common benign uterine condition that can cause dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) and infertility. Management may involve medication, radiological procedures or surgery. Hormonal treatment is presented as the initial approach because it can improve symptoms and reduce uterine size. UAE, HIFU, RFA and hysteroscopy may be considered when medication is ineffective. Hysterectomy remains the only definitive treatment, although interest in preserving the uterus has increased. Conservative surgery can improve AUB and pelvic pain and reduce uterine volume, but it carries postoperative and obstetric risks. Because cytoreductive surgery can be technically demanding, it should be undertaken by experienced surgeons in dedicated centers, particularly when endometriosis is also present.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Adenomyosis consists of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium. It can produce diffuse uterine enlargement or a focal lesion. Diagnosis was historically made by examining hysterectomy specimens from peri-menopausal women treated for chronic pelvic pain and AUB; advances in imaging now permit recognition in younger women of reproductive age. Possible presentations include dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, AUB and infertility, although about one third of cases may have no symptoms. Ultrasound-unit data indicate that about 21% of the general population has sonographic signs of adenomyosis; the proportion is higher among women undergoing assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs). Adenomyosis frequently occurs alongside endometriosis, uterine myomas or congenital uterine abnormalities. Across studies, its coexistence with endometriosis on Trans-Vaginal Ultrasound (TVUS) and magnetic resonance imaging ranges between 21.2% and 89.4%. The association appears particularly strong with severe dysmenorrhea and deep endometriosis (DE). A cited study of preoperative ultrasound in reproductive-age women undergoing laparoscopy for pelvic pain found a strong correlation with stage IV endometriosis. Older age and greater gravidity and parity are also often reported when the two conditions coexist. Women with both conditions have poorer quality of life (Qol) and sexual functioning. Symptoms, age and fertility wishes inform the choice among medical, radiological and surgical care.

document_sections.heading: 2. Adenomyosis: the medical treatment
document_sections.content: There are currently no established adenomyosis treatment guidelines, and treatments used for it are off-label, as with endometriosis. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and tranexamic acid have limited roles, chiefly for mild symptoms or exacerbations during hormonal therapy. Progestins, particularly LNG-IUS and dienogest, are commonly used and can relieve symptoms and decrease uterine size. Adenomyotic tissue shows reduced expression of progesterone receptors (PR) B, as occurs in endometriosis, yet it can respond well to a high intrauterine progestin dose. LNG-IUS is described as a highly effective, safe contraceptive approved for continuous use for up to 6 years. Its possible effects on adenomyosis-related dysmenorrhea and AUB involve both direct action on lesions and modulation of altered endometrial factors. Local LNG lowers estrogen-receptor expression, leading to decidualization and atrophy of ectopic endometrium and limiting further estrogen stimulation. LNG-IUS has been associated with quality-of-life gains comparable to those of more invasive surgery, substantial relief of pelvic pain and AUB, and few local or systemic adverse effects. Uterine vascularity and symptoms can improve rapidly, but uterine-volume reduction begins 2 years after insertion. Spontaneous expulsion is related to uterine size and menstrual blood loss; treatment failure is significantly more frequent when uterine volume exceeds 150 mL. Dienogest (DNG) can reduce uterine volume and uterine blood flow and relieve symptoms. Reported adverse effects in some treated patients include vaginal dryness, reduced libido and alopecia. DNG does not provide complete contraception; when adverse effects are severe or a contraceptive pill is needed, it can be combined with 30 μg of ethinylestradiol. The characteristic progesterone resistance of adenomyotic endometrium and stroma may cause the benefit of progestins to diminish progressively. Combined oral contraceptives (COC) and the progestin only pill (POP) are also used off-label for symptom control. They produce a pregnancy-like hormonal state followed by decidualization and atrophy of the endometrium and adenomyotic lesions; amenorrhea or lighter menstruation can ease dysmenorrhea. GnRH-a are used as second-line treatment if progestins fail or cannot be tolerated. They initially cause a flare-up, then suppress FSH and LH secretion and ovarian sex-steroid production, reducing uterine volume and severe dysmenorrhea. Oral GnRH-ants block pituitary GnRH receptors and immediately suppress reproductive function through inhibition of adenohypophyseal FSH and LH secretion. elagolix, relugolix and linzagolix are under consideration for endometriosis and uterine leiomyomas, and successful use of linzagolix in adenomyosis has been reported. Table 1 summarizes medical, radiological and surgical options, their proposed actions or indications, advantages and cited evidence.

document_sections.heading: 3. Adenomyosis: the radiological treatment
document_sections.content: When medication fails, proposed interventions include uterine artery embolization (UAE) and high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU). Following positive randomized-trial findings for UAE in uterine leiomyoma, case series investigated it for symptomatic adenomyosis. During the first year after UAE, AUB and dysmenorrhea appear to improve to a similar degree. Reported postprocedural findings include a uterine-volume reduction of 50% at 12 months after treatment and areas of devascularization; necrosis of varying extent has been proposed as a reason for symptom reduction or elimination. HIFU produces targeted thermal coagulation of adenomyotic tissue. Local thermal destruction of ectopic endometrium is intended to interrupt the release of bleeding and inflammatory mediators associated with cyclic ovarian-hormone responses. Its potential as a substitute for invasive surgery is less established. Precise targeting can create localized tissue necrosis without surgery. Studies report that efficacy and recurrence depend on disease type, with better results in focal than diffuse adenomyosis. HIFU is associated with symptom relief and significant improvement in Qol. Blood-flow signals within adenomyotic tissue fall significantly after treatment, alongside symptom improvement at 6 months; subsequent LNG-IUS use can improve clinical outcomes. Available data describe a significant reduction in menstrual volume at 2 years of follow-up and complete symptom relief in 68% of women treated with HIFU. Studies have assessed HIFU safety, although serious complications include skin burns and nerve injury. Fertility is an important consideration: ultrasound or MRI guidance permits precise lesion ablation intended to preserve adjacent myometrium and endometrium. Table 2 summarizes reports on UAE and HIFU, including short- and long-term outcomes, HIFU with GnRh-a or LNG-IUD, and safety. Table 1 describes a possible adverse effect of HIFU on fertility, whereas the discussion of guided ablation emphasizes preservation of surrounding tissue.

document_sections.heading: 4. Adenomyosis: the surgical treatment
document_sections.content: Hysterectomy has traditionally been the surgical treatment and remains the only definitive option; uterus-preserving procedures have become more available. Hyams introduced adenomyomectomy in 1952. For focal disease, the adenomyoma is separated from healthy myometrium and removed, although its poorly defined boundary makes this more difficult than myomectomy. Cytoreductive surgery can address focal or diffuse disease by extensively removing adenomyotic foci together with substantial healthy myometrium. Partial and complete approaches have been developed to access the lesion. Partial wedge resection identifies the seromuscolar layer over the disease and removes part of the serosa and adenomyotic tissue. One modification uses a transverse H incision at the uterine fundus, removes diseased tissue in thin slices, sutures the myometrium in one or two layers and closes serosal flaps with interrupted subserosal sutures. It can be performed by laparoscopy or laparotomy. The triple-flap method was devised as a complete cytoreductive procedure intended to support a possible later pregnancy. It divides the uterus in the mid-sagittal plane to the endometrium, removes the adenomyotic tissue completely, then closes the cavity, the muscle and serosa on one side, and the seromuscolar layer from the opposite side as three successive flaps. Laparotomy is preferred because tissue removal requires hand palpation and suturing is difficult. Asymmetric dissection is another complete approach: a longitudinal uterine incision, diagonal myometrial dissection and transverse opening of the uterine cavity are followed by cavity closure and reconstruction using one uterine side to cover the other. Conservative surgery appears to improve pelvic pain (>70% at 12 months) and AUB (>70% at 12 months), with uterine volume estimated to decrease by a factor of 3.1; differences among procedures do not appear significant. Osada et al. reported a uterine rupture rate of 5% during pregnancy after adenomyomectomy. Abortion, other pregnancy complications and placentation abnormalities, including placenta previa and placenta accreta spectrum, have also been described, though without high prevalence. Uterus-preserving surgery may suit women with repeated medical-treatment failures who wish to retain the uterus. Because no conservative operation has been demonstrated superior, the approach should be individualized using patient needs and preoperative pelvic ultrasound and MRI assessment of disease location and extent. Particularly in diffuse disease, adequate lesion removal and sound uterine-wall reconstruction are important. Difficult excision and suturing create a potentially appreciable risk of uterine rupture during pregnancy. Surgeons should avoid heat damage to incision edges because it raises the risk of suture dehiscence. Coexisting pelvic endometriosis, especially DE, or uterine myomas may require simultaneous, complex multidisciplinary treatment.

document_sections.heading: 5. Adenomyosis: radiofrequency ablation
document_sections.content: Laparoscopic radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is an alternative for premenopausal patients with symptomatic focal adenomyosis resistant to hormonal treatment; ultrasound-guided RFA is another option. In the laparoscopic procedure, a needle electrode with an extendible prong is guided into nodular adenomyosis, targeting 98 ◦C. The needle tract is then coagulated for hemostasis. Electrode-generated heat causes thermal fixation and coagulative necrosis while preserving cellular architecture. Peripheral tissue changes, contraction and dehydration further reduce uterine volume; thermal effects also decrease expression of ER and PR. Across studies, reported uterine-volume reductions range from 41% to 57%. Severe complications such as perforation, infection and thermal injury to abdominal organs are uncommon, while vaginal discharge, abdominal pain and low-grade fever are reported more often. RFA is associated with clinically meaningful short-term improvement in dysmenorrhea, dyschezia, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, bulk symptoms and AUB, resembling the benefit of conventional uterus-preserving surgery. It has allowed hysterectomy to be avoided in several cases. Evidence concerning AUB effectiveness, uterine morphological changes, pregnancy and fertility remains inconclusive.

document_sections.heading: 6. Adenomyosis: hysteroscopic treatment
document_sections.content: Several hysteroscopic appearances have been linked to adenomyosis, but the method's diagnostic role is uncertain because it does not assess the deeper myometrium commonly involved. Hysteroscopic treatment has been proposed for focal or diffuse disease near the endometrium; it is not considered appropriate for deeper lesions. A focal lesion less than 1.5 cm and close to the endometrial cavity may be enucleated in an ambulatory setting with mechanical instruments or bipolar electrodes, similarly to a submucosal myoma. Resectoscopic treatment may be feasible for larger lesions or diffuse superficial disease, including in an office setting when a mini-resectoscope is available. Endometrial or endo-myometrial ablation may be performed for women who do not desire future pregnancy. Although medical therapy appears more effective for adenomyosis-related symptoms, improvement in dysmenorrhea and AUB is described in about 50% of hysteroscopically treated patients.

document_sections.heading: 7. Conclusions
document_sections.content: Conservative medical, radiological and surgical treatments can relieve AUB and pelvic pain and reduce uterine volume. Hormonal medication is considered the primary approach during reproductive life; radiological or conservative surgical treatment is considered when medication fails. Conservative operations are technically complex, and open surgery may sometimes be preferable because finger palpation helps identify the boundary between adenomyosis and healthy myometrium. Published findings suggest that surgical, early postoperative and pregnancy complications, including hematomas, suture anastomotic leakage and adhesions, do not appear particularly frequent after either laparoscopy or laparotomy. Temporary uterine-artery occlusion or ligation and intramyometrial vasopressin or oxytocin injection have been proposed to reduce intraoperative blood loss and may be options in some cases. Reported complication rates may be underestimated because the procedures come mainly from highly experienced centers with limited bleeding, reliable suturing and reduced bowel and urinary injury. Coexisting pelvic endometriosis, especially DE, and uterine myomas often require concurrent multidisciplinary care. Some authors question whether outcomes from expert centers apply to general gynecological practice and caution surgeons with limited experience against reproducing these complex procedures. The authors conclude that experienced surgeons in dedicated centers should perform conservative adenomyosis surgery, particularly for laparoscopy or concomitant endometriosis. For selected premenopausal women with symptomatic focal disease resistant to hormonal treatment, RFA or hysteroscopy may offer alternatives.

document_sections.heading: Practice Points.
document_sections.content: Hormonal and non-hormonal therapy are presented as the first approach to adenomyosis. The practice points describe progestins, including LNG-IUS and dienogest, GnRH-a and oral GnRH-ants as first-line treatments that can substantially improve symptoms and reduce uterine volume; elsewhere, the article specifies GnRH-a as second-line treatment when progestins fail or are not tolerated. UAE, HIFU, RFA and hysteroscopy are presented as alternatives after medical-treatment failure. Conservative surgery can improve AUB and pelvic pain and decrease uterine volume when medication fails, but limited numbers of patients may experience obstetric complications, including abortion, pregnancy complications or placentation abnormalities. Hysterectomy is the only definitive surgical treatment for premenopausal patients who do not wish to retain the uterus. Because conservative operations are often technically complex and endometriosis frequently coexists, they should be performed by experienced surgeons in dedicated centers.

document_sections.heading: Research agenda.
document_sections.content: The authors propose comparing conservative surgical techniques for treatment outcomes, complications and obstetric outcomes; assessing their long-term effects, particularly on AUB and pelvic pain; comparing conservative surgery with medical treatment, especially newer GnRH antagonists; and comparing it with radiological procedures, particularly Radiofrequency Ablation.
